lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality, which readers are not meant to weigh.
items.because: They are unrelated to qualifications and introduce protected personal information.

items.says: The experience entries are not ordered newest-first.
items.because: Showing Pinecrest before the more recent Brightcart role makes the chronology harder to scan.

items.says: Education appears before the more decision-relevant professional experience.
items.because: With five years of relevant work, recruiters should encounter the candidate's professional level before the degree.

items.says: “Owned the claims backlog report” does not identify the substantive work performed.
items.because: Ownership could mean distribution, production, validation, or analytical maintenance.

items.says: “The weekly numbers the claims managers used” does not say what action or result the reporting supported.
The entry's strongest operational achievement is not presented first.
items.because: The hold-time reduction is its clearest connection between analysis and an operating result.

items.says: “Analyzed 18 months of call-center data” does not say how the staffing pattern was identified.
“My findings” does not fit the résumé's phrase-based style.
The administrative task list separates the automation from its 10-hour result and buries the achievement.
items.because: Unrelated duties obscure which work produced the saving and distract from the fraud extract's value.

items.says: “Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract” does not explain the technical contribution.
items.because: The reader cannot distinguish scripting or workflow development from simple scheduling.

items.says: “Improved reporting efficiency by 90%” does not define the metric that improved.
items.because: The unclear denominator makes the large percentage difficult to evaluate or trust.

items.says: “By 90% by” is repetitive.
The SQL join is reversed for finding customers with no orders.
items.because: Keeping orders as the left table identifies orders without matching customers, not customers without orders.

items.says: The finding's scale or business consequence is not stated.
“Wrote data-quality checks” does not identify the conditions tested.
“Presented the quarterly customer review” does not identify the analysis behind the recommendations.
items.because: Presentation alone could read as coordination rather than the analytical work that generated the funded recommendations.

items.says: The national conversion rate is calculated incorrectly as an unweighted average of regional rates.
items.because: It requires total conversions divided by total traffic, or rates weighted by regional traffic.

items.says: The line does not say what the corrected metric informed.
The retention-dashboard bullet buries its strongest result.
items.because: The rise in 90-day repeat purchase is more compelling than the dashboard's scale alone.

items.says: “Built the weekly retention dashboard” does not identify the logic used to define or track retention.
items.because: The line does not show how customer records became an actionable lapsed-buyer audience.

items.says: “That marketing used” can grammatically modify the customers rather than the dashboard.
“12% mean absolute error” misstates the forecasting metric.
items.because: Mean absolute error uses demand units, while a percentage requires a percentage-based or normalized metric.

items.says: “Modeled hourly bike-share demand” does not identify the forecasting approach.
items.because: The bullet does not distinguish a substantive forecasting method from a basic projection.

items.says: The reported forecast error has no baseline comparison.
The line does not identify the forecast-based intervention that produced the reduction.
items.because: Saying the forecast was compared with a schedule does not show whether the candidate generated recommendations, optimized a schedule, or merely evaluated a plan.

items.says: The project's strongest simulated operating result is not presented first.
items.because: The reduction in empty-station hours is its clearest evidence of potential operational value.

items.says: “Last summer” is an unstable and increasingly ambiguous date reference.
“Empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week” attaches the weekly qualifier awkwardly.
“Which” does not clarify whether the city linked the write-up alone or both deliverables.
“Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day” does not identify the technique or tool used.
Matching repeat visitors does not by itself produce a count of unique households.
items.because: Several individuals can belong to one household, so a household count needs an identifier or household-level matching method.

items.says: The line does not explain how handwritten records were standardized or matched.
items.because: Without the rules or tooling, a reader cannot assess the data-quality skill needed to reconcile 9,000 logs.

items.says: The first unique-person or household count is not connected to a downstream decision or requirement.
The claim about 2.4 million shoppers and repeat purchases is misattributed to the food-pantry project.
items.because: Its scale, result, and retail terms duplicate Brightcart's claim and contradict the pantry entry's focus.

items.says: “That raised repeat purchases” implies the dashboard directly caused the outcome without explaining the action it enabled.
items.because: A dashboard supports decisions, so the intervening use is needed to assess attribution.

items.says: “Raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter” does not define the measure or comparison point.
items.because: The reader cannot tell the type of increase or the retention window, making its magnitude impossible to verify or compare.
